In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the physical mechanisms of degradation in power GaAs MESFTs.
the development of a new generation of power GaAs FETs with improved reliability and performance.
the study of the electrical characteristics of power GaA MESFETs under accelerated aging conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the parasitic FET is a result of a thermally induced localized microreaction between the gate and source (drain).
a parasitic FTE is formed in power GaAs MESFTTs due to the occurrence of localized burn-out phenomena, which can be enhanced by high temperature operation.
the parasitic ungated MESFET is not an intrinsic device effect but rather an extrinsic device effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the onset of a parasitically gated FET is a result of the thermal instability of the gate metal-Gallium arsenide interface.
we have been able to demonstrate the presence of parasitic FETs and the mechanism for their formation.
the gate-to-source/drain diode characteristics can be used as a sensitive tool for the detection of microreactions and for the assessment of the reliability of GaAs MESFETS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the onset of parasitic FETs can be used as an indicator of microreactions in the gate region.
the onset of parasitic FETs is an indicator of the onset of burn-out phenomena, which are responsible for the degradation of the device characteristics.
the parasitic FET can be used as a sensitive probe of the thermal stability of the power device.
